name: Colin Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most weekdays I'm at Northlight, a small studio on the ring road that makes music for adverts and radio jingles. Gregor runs it, and I'm the house bass player, so I sit in the live room and play whatever line he hums at me until it fits a thirty-second spot for a car dealer or a carpet sale. I'm honestly not the best player he could get, I still fluff takes, but I'm cheap and I turn up. Friday and Saturday nights I play bass in a covers band called The Late Shift, pubs and the odd wedding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you in it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The late nights wear me out, loading the van at one in the morning and still being at the studio at ten. What keeps me in it is the moment a take clicks and Gregor just nods through the glass. My girlfriend Hanne works shifts as a nurse, so we see each other in the gaps. We've got about four months of rent put aside, which is more than most musicians I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the people I know were losing sleep over computers writing songs, and if it turns out to be a fancier spellcheck, fine. I'd probably post something smug about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't mean I'm safe, because the studio was already struggling before anyone said AI. Ad budgets have been tight for years and local shops don't buy radio spots like they used to. So I'd still be the cheap bass player in a shrinking room, just without a robot to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Northlight and keep the Late Shift going, because that's the money. I'd try to get a second weekday gig, maybe depping for other bands, which means filling in when their player is ill. And I'd keep putting a bit by every month so the four months doesn't drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not relaxed. I still check the studio diary every Monday to see how many sessions are booked. A thin week makes my stomach drop, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you check that diary on Monday, what does a bad week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad week is two sessions instead of five, and that's maybe a third of my pay gone. Gregor pays per session, not a wage. A slow month at the jingle studio already means Hanne (his girlfriend) covers more of the rent, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd want to change, if nothing big happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a proper rate card, a set price per session that every studio sticks to. The union has one, but most small places ignore it. If nothing big happens with AI, that's still the fight worth having.

say: I'd tell people the **AI scare** was overblown and computers can't really play bass.
I'd probably post something **smug** about being right all along.
think: The jingle studio was **already struggling** before AI, because local ad budgets keep shrinking.
A thin week of **two sessions** cuts about a third of my pay.
do: Keep playing at **Northlight** on weekdays and with the covers band at weekends.
Look for **depping** work, filling in for other bands' bass players.
Keep **saving monthly** so the four-month cushion stays intact.
feel: **Relieved** that AI stalled, but still tense about each week's **bookings**.
S0.quote: A slow month at the jingle studio already means Hanne (his girlfriend) covers more of the rent, and I hate that.
fieldNote: He's paid **per session**, so his income swings with the studio diary, not with AI.
Guilt about his girlfriend **covering rent** came up quickly and sounded sharp.
His instinct is a **union rate card**, even in the calm scenario.

steps.text: Keep weekday bass sessions at the jingle studio and weekend covers gigs
Ask other local bands about depping when their bassist is off
Put a fixed amount aside each month to hold four months' rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that bosses will use anything to pay us less. I'd share the union's posts about fair pay for session players. And I'd tell my mates in other bands to stop putting their stems online for free, because that's what trains these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think jingles are the first thing to go. A car dealer doesn't care if a real person played the bass on a thirty-second spot. If Gregor can type 'upbeat funk, cheap' into a box and get it in a minute, he's going to, and I'd do the same in his shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the musicians' union properly, not just read their posts, and go to the branch meetings. I'd try to get more pub and wedding gigs, because people still want a band in the room. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff myself; I don't trust it and I don't want to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit embarrassed, because I'm not good enough to be the player they keep. The good session players will be fine for a while. It's people like me at the bottom who go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete, who does the drums, has been there twenty years and has nothing else. I'm twenty-seven, I can carry amps or work a bar if I have to. Old Pete (the studio drummer) has played on every jingle this town has heard since 2005, and a computer would replace him in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the tools. If Gregor asked you to, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no the first time. If he made it the only way to keep my sessions, I'd probably do the least I could and hate it. I know that's not a great plan.

say: I'd say **bosses** will use AI as an excuse to pay musicians less.
I'd tell friends to stop sharing their **stems** online for free.
think: **Jingles** are the first work to go, because clients won't pay for a real bassist.
Weaker players like me at the **bottom** get cut before the good ones.
do: Join the **musicians' union** as a full member and attend branch meetings.
Chase more **pub and wedding** gigs, where people still want a live band.
Refuse to learn the **AI tools** unless forced to keep sessions.
feel: **Angry** at the studio owners and **embarrassed** about being easy to replace.
S1.quote: Old Pete (the studio drummer) has played on every jingle this town has heard since 2005, and a computer would replace him in a week.
fieldNote: He expects his **studio sessions** to shrink and knows he's not the player they'd keep.
His worry for **Pete**, the older drummer, felt more raw than worry for himself.
He admits refusing the tools is a **weak plan**, but sticks with it.

steps.text: Join the musicians' union as a paying member and attend branch meetings
Ring pub landlords and wedding agents to book more Late Shift gigs
Keep playing studio sessions for as long as Gregor books them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, not after. Tax the companies making the stuff and pay people while they work out what's next. I'd be loud about it online, probably louder than is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. The studio is screen work really, so I reckon Gregor closes Northlight inside a year, or it becomes him and a laptop. By 2028 my bass would be worth more on a second-hand site than my playing is worth to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop spending on gear and build the savings past four months if I could. I'd lean on the Late Shift and try to get a regular bar job alongside it. I'd sign every petition going and go to whatever protests the union organises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Not panicking, because I've got some money and Hanne's job is safe, nurses aren't going anywhere. But it feels like the floor goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots for hands-on work come about three years later. Does that give live playing some breathing room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for live gigs, yeah, a robot isn't standing in a pub playing Mr Brightside by 2028. But if every pub can play a perfect AI band through the speakers for free, why pay us two hundred quid? The breathing room is only real if people still want humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hanne talk about at the kitchen table that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I should give up on music and train for something steady. She'd say do what makes you happy, and I'd say happy doesn't pay half the rent. We'd probably end up talking about whether I should look at hospital porter jobs where she works.

say: I'd demand the **government** tax AI firms and pay workers while they adjust.
I'd be **loud online**, probably louder than is good for me.
think: Northlight is mostly **screen work**, so the studio likely closes within a year.
Live gigs only survive if pubs still choose **real musicians** over free AI music.
do: Stop buying **gear** and push savings past four months.
Take a regular **bar job** alongside the covers band.
Sign **petitions** and turn out for union protests.
feel: **Scared** that the floor is going, but steadied by his girlfriend's **nursing job**.
S2.quote: By 2028 my bass would be worth more on a second-hand site than my playing is worth to anyone.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the studio income** within a year and said so plainly.
His girlfriend's **secure job** is what stops him from panicking.
The talk turned to **hospital porter** work, a big step for someone so attached to music.

steps.text: Stop buying music gear and add to the rent savings
Apply for a regular bar job to sit alongside weekend gigs
Go to union protests and sign petitions for an AI tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: tax it, share it, protect workers. With five years you can't say nobody saw it coming, so I'd be asking why the government isn't building something now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but it lands in the same place for me. I'd get maybe three more years of jingles, then nothing. Live playing might hold till the robots, around 2034, if people still care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably start a part-time course in something practical, maybe sound engineering for live venues, because someone still has to rig a PA. I'd keep the band going and put more into savings each month. I'd stay active in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a slow leak. It's not as sharp as the two-year one, but I'd be checking for the drip every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why live sound rather than something outside music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's hands-on and it keeps me in venues with musicians. I know the gear already from loading in. Somebody has to climb the ladder and fix the speaker at the Crown pub when it cuts out mid-song.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if live sound gets automated a few years after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in my mid-thirties starting again, which scares me. I'd hope by then there's some proper support from the government. I don't really have a plan for that bit.

say: I'd ask why the **government** isn't preparing when there's five years' warning.
I'd keep pushing to **tax and share** what AI firms earn.
think: I'd get about **three more years** of jingle sessions before they disappear.
Live playing might last until robots arrive in **2034**, if people care.
do: Start a **part-time course** in live sound engineering for venues.
Keep the **covers band** going and save more each month.
feel: A steady, **uneasy** feeling, like a **slow leak** he checks weekly.
S3.quote: Somebody has to climb the ladder and fix the speaker at the Crown pub when it cuts out mid-song.
fieldNote: Even with five years he expects to **lose the jingle work**, just later.
He reaches for **live sound** because it's hands-on and keeps him near musicians.
He has **no plan** for when robots arrive and admits it.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time live sound engineering course at the local college
Add more each month to savings while jingle sessions last
Stay active in the musicians' union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do it properly, so no excuses. Retraining money, a guaranteed income, all of it. I'd say it at union meetings and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real chance for me. I'm twenty-seven, so I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands and forty when robots come. That's time to get properly good at something, maybe even at bass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the live sound course over two years and start doing venue work at weekends. I'd keep playing and actually practise, which I'm lazy about. And Hanne and I might finally look at saving for a deposit, since there'd be time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit. Still worried, because it's the same end point, but it doesn't feel like a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually practise this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the cheap players go first. If I'm still the weakest bassist in town in 2036, I'm done. Ten years is long enough to stop being the cheapest bass player in town and start being the one people ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be a musician in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but maybe as one part of the week, not all of it. Sound work Monday to Thursday, playing at the weekend. I'd rather be a part-time musician who eats than a full-time one who doesn't.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for governments to skip retraining money.
I'd push for a **guaranteed income** at union meetings and online.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when AGI lands, which is time to build real skills.
The same end point still comes, so the jingle work goes **eventually**.
do: Finish a **live sound** course over two years and work venues at weekends.
Practise **bass** properly so I'm not the cheapest player in town.
Start saving towards a **house deposit** with Hanne.
feel: **Hopeful** for once, though the same **end point** still worries him.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to stop being the cheapest bass player in town and start being the one people ask for.
fieldNote: The **decade of warning** turns his anger into something like a plan.
He admits being **lazy about practice** and links it straight to who gets cut.
He still expects music to become **part-time** for him.

steps.text: Complete a two-year live sound course and take weekend venue shifts
Practise bass every weekday morning before studio sessions
Open a joint deposit savings account with Hanne

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for me to learn anything new, and the studio would go before I'd even started. What would help is the government paying for retraining and covering some wages while people switch, and studios being made to pay the union rate while they still use us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the stems thing. Every musician I know has uploaded their tracks somewhere for free, and that's what these companies trained on. Someone should have to pay for that, and some of that money should come back to people like Pete.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be a part-time musician who eats than a full-time one who doesn't.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old bass player** at a small jingle studio who plays pub gigs at weekends.
He's paid **per session**, has about four months saved and shares rent with his nurse girlfriend, Hanne.
He's **left-leaning** and turns to the union and government first, and refuses to use AI tools.
He expects **jingle work** to vanish in every strong scenario and only plans properly when given a decade.
He worries more for **Pete**, the older studio drummer, than he lets on about himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the studio would close before he could learn anything new.
whatWouldHelp: **Government-paid retraining** and wage support while people switch work.
Studios paying the **union rate** and AI firms paying musicians whose tracks they **trained on**.
